sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Transformers (Vaswani et al., 2017) have been highly successful in part because their architecture is well suited to eﬀicient gradient-based optimization on modern GPUs (Hooker, 2021; Dao, 2024). However, this advantage does not necessarily carry over to weight-space programming (WSP), where large language model (LLM) directly writes the weights of separate target model without gradient-based training or data fitting (Takehi et al., 2026). This shift raises central question. Should weight-space programming keep the Transformer? To answer this question, we provide minimal guidance, giving each LLM only ten labeled questions and an execution sandbox. Within this setup, we evaluate two regimes, (i) performing WSP on diverse released architectures (Transformers, state-space models (Gu et al., 2022), and RNNs (Elman, 1990)) from random initialization, and (ii) allowing the LLM to choose and design the target architecture from scratch. We conduct our evaluation primarily on ARC multiple-choice science questions (Clark et al., 2018) across three frontier LLMs, namely Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic, 2026), GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI, 2026a), and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b). When free to choose the structure, the LLMs do not build Transformers; an LLM-designed model achieves higher ARC test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800 fewer parameters. We analyze in detail how these LLM-designed models are constructed, as building them differs from adjusting parameters via gradient descent. The LLM first expresses domain facts as plain-text sentences and writes build script that converts each sentence into row of sparse table. fixed lookup procedure then reads the table, matching tokens from the question and each candidate option against its rows to select the highest-scoring answer. All three LLMs converge on this design without using attention, MLPs, or dense embeddings. This structure is well suited to writing weights without gradients because every prediction traces back to specific rows, and editing row affects only the questions that rely on it. Empirically, in Claude Opus 5.5s models, retaining only the single best-matching row per option nearly matches full-model accuracy, and deleting row alters roughly one prediction out of all test questions. By contrast, when Claude Opus 5.5 writes the same facts into Transformer, it underperforms plain keyword search (BM25) over the raw sentences, which is consistent with interference between dense keys. Viewed as associative memories (Zhong et al., 2025; Wang, 2026), the sparse table pairs few-token keys with hard top-row selection, whereas the Transformer relies on dense, overlapping keys and soft attention. However, an LLM-designed model scores every stored fact for every question, so inference slows down as the writer adds facts, and it launches many GPU kernels per question. Most of these models therefore run slower on GPU than same-sized Transformer. Building on our analysis, we propose an associative-memory-based model that retains the written table while reading only fixed number of rows per question; it stays within about three percentage points of the LLM-designed models accuracy while answering up to 17 faster on GPU than the same-sized Transformer. We test how well these findings generalize beyond random initialization and multiplechoice science questions, extending our evaluation to pretrained weights, math questions, open-ended generation, and vision tasks. Finally, while pretrained LLMs remain far more accurate overall, we clarify the practical boundaries of current WSP and outline key limitations and future directions for the paradigm.

sections.title: 3.4 Our associative-memory-based model
sections.content: LLM-designed models score every stored fact for every question (Equation (2)), so work per question grows with the number of written facts, and they launch many GPU kernels; on GPU, most run slower than same-sized Transformer (Figure 4). We therefore design an associative-memory-based model that preserves line-by-line writing (Figure 2c). Given our fixed forward pass along with its weight names and tensor shapes, the LLM writes word list, plain-text files in line formats of its choice, and build script that compiles them into two tables. Per question, the forward pass reads only 120 pair-table rows and computes single product with concept table A, keeping per-question cost independent of fact count for given concept vocabulary (Section 6 analyzes GPU speed and accuracy). To populate the two tables, the LLMs build script compiles written lines such as cues with supported answers, terms with definition words, and parents with children. Concept table is first-order memory holding how strongly concept alone recalls concept b, while the pair table is second-order memory holding the concepts that pair of concepts (a, b), written with < b, recalls together. Each pair maps directly to row h(a, b) = (ap + b) mod for fixed prime and table height H, so the forward pass computes the row address and searches nothing. From questions concept vector q, the = 16 strongest concepts form the set P(q) of 120 pairs. In Claude Opus 5.5s first-generation model, 40,312 words map to 3,805 concepts, table holds 2.06 million nonzero entries, and the pair table uses = 1,048,576 rows, each storing up to 40 recalled concept IDs and weights. In the LLMdesigned model, related word forms such as bird, birds, and birds, or larger, bigger, and big, share one concept, so the 4,288 written facts match whatever form the question uses. Each fact row is matched with both the question and an option, and their product gives the rows support. sections.title: 4 Results
sections.content: Within weight-space programming, letting the LLM design the model structure outperforms fixing standard architecture  (Table 3)  . Across all three LLMs, LLM-designed models achieve higher ARC test accuracy with far fewer parameters than released architectures, including Transformers, written from random initialization. Our associativememory-based model (Section 3.4) retains this advantage over fixed architectures across all three LLMs. Refining the designed models across generations raises accuracy further, reaching 54.4% in the strongest lineage. Without pretraining, these written models also surpass gradient descent. Released architectures trained by gradient descent from the same random initializations stay near random guessing even on the full training set, and small networks trained from scratch at the scale of the LLM-designed models likewise fall well short. sections.title: 5 Why the LLMs choose this structure
sections.content: Sparse tables satisfy both properties from Section 3.2 by tracing each answer to single written line and limiting line removal to far fewer changed answers than in written Transformer. When compiled into Transformer, however, the same content underperforms plain search over the written text, and edits no longer reliably stay local. 5.1 Testing the two properties Does an answer trace to one line? To test whether each prediction relies on single stored statement, we keep only the single best-matching fact for each option and drop every other score. In the LLM-designed model, the full model reaches 50.8% test accuracy, and scoring each option from its single best-matching fact alone reaches 49.1%  (Table 4)  . Accuracy comes mostly from the best written fact for each option. Does an edit stay local? We remove one written line, rebuild the model, and compare it with the unchanged model on the test set for 40 random lines per model; rebuilding an unchanged model changes nothing. In eager execution, log-log GPU time correlates more closely with kernels per question (r = 0.95) than with non-zero count. At each models fastest mode, time tracks non-zero count more closely (correlation 0.84 against 0.64). Across 46 LLM-designed variants (Figure 4a), only one beats same-sized Transformer at its fastest input, and the median is 9.4 slower. These designs score every fact for every question, although in Claude Opus 5.5s lineage about one fact in seven shares word with the question on average. They build an intermediate table with one entry per question, option, and fact, passing over that table several times. Over generations, the LLM adds scoring steps and rule modules, so kernels per question grow from 13 in Claude Opus 5.5s first generation to 118 in its fifth. Many designs build or transpose sparse tables inside the forward pass, which prevents capture as CUDA graph, the optimization that removes kernel launch overhead. Cost grows with the number of facts times the number of scoring passes, and our associative-memory-based model (Section 3.4) removes this growth. 6.2 What the architecture has to keep faster design must keep what makes weights writable without gradients (a line as the unit, nameable meaning for every entry, and sparse keys) and must stop scoring every fact for every question. sections.title: 6.4 Scaling and capacity
sections.content: In eager execution on synthetic tables with the shape of the written models, time per question stays at 0.012 ms on the GPU while the pair table grows from 3 million to 1 billion non-zero values, whereas same-sized Transformer goes from 0.044 ms to 14.5 ms. Time instead grows with the number of concepts. With the concept table stored densely, as in the written models, the model becomes slower than Transformer between about 15,000 and 32,000 concepts, while variant that reads the concept table as row lists stays faster up to about 100,000 concepts. In the first-generation model, sharing rows of the pair table costs no accuracy down to 65,536 rows (49.6% at 1,048,576 rows and 49.8% at 65,536). Section gives the scaling curves and the capacity results.

sections.title: 7 Further experiments
sections.content: This section asks how far our findings go beyond random initialization and multiple-choice science questions. Wherever the LLM designs the model, it keeps written tables and fixed reader, adding rule modules when needed and adapting what row holds to the task. 7.1 WSP of pretrained weights Starting from released pretrained checkpoint instead of random initialization, WSP behaves differently. In most runs (48 of 87 across the three LLMs), the LLM changes under 1% of the weights. Most of these edits calibrate how the answer letter is read out or move science-word embeddings toward written definitions, and accuracy stays within one point of the checkpoints in 43 of these 48 runs. In 30 runs, the LLM overwrites the checkpoint, in 29 with hand-written fact or rule model and one with hand-built similarity circuit. Most overwrites (19 of 30) are on checkpoints near chance. The exceptions are GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra runs on the masked-language encoders UltraBERT and ModernBERT-large, which start above chance and lose accuracy when overwritten. The remaining nine keep the checkpoint and rewire it so that its own signal selects the answer letter. Checkpoints above 72% are never overwritten. Per-checkpoint results are in Section F.1. 7.2 Other benchmarks We run models written for ARC unchanged on other four-option benchmarks. On SciQ (Welbl et al., 2017), science questions of the same level, the LLM-designed and associative-memory-based models both reach 47.7% in generation 1 and 50.1% in generation 5, within about four points of ARC. Accuracy is 30% to 36% on OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018) and near 25% chance on MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021). This pattern is consistent with Claude Opus 5.5 having written elementary science, matching SciQ rather than OpenBookQA or MMLU. Section F.2 gives details. 7.3 Text generation tasks We ask the LLM for models that produce text answers instead of choosing an option, extracting passage span on SQuAD 1.1 (Rajpurkar et al., 2016) or writing an answer one word at time on SciQ. The structure does not change in kind. For each task, Claude Opus 5.5 designs new model of written lookup tables read by fixed procedure, changing only what row holds, with word lists and reading procedure for SQuAD and answers with the words of questions about them for SciQ. Generation here means reading out stored answer. In Table 8, its LLM-designed model scores above the written Transformer and the same Transformer trained by gradient descent on all usable training items on both tasks. Details are in Section F.3. 7.4 Several tasks at once We also test single task statement that names several kinds of items at once, giving ten multiple-choice examples each from ARC, MMLU, and MathBench (Liu et al., 2024) and ten 11 Preprint. On CNN/DailyMail, the first-sentence copiers of all three LLMs score below copying the first three sentences of the article (24.9 ROUGE-L). sections.title: 8 Limitations and future work
sections.content: Recall without learned representations. The multiple-choice and SciQ table models, our associative-memory-based model, and the released architectures written from random initialization answer by recalling facts the LLM wrote. None chains facts across steps or composes long answer. ARC-Challenge accuracy stays near 38% while ARC-Easy reaches 63%  (Table 3)  . Run unchanged, models written for ARC stay at chance on MMLU. On SQuAD the written models extract spans with word lists, and some written models compute, including arithmetic in the models written for several tasks at once or with no task named (Section 7). Written models store what the LLM states and learn no representations of their own. natural next step is weight-space programming that builds representations and acquires knowledge beyond the facts writer can state. Scope of the claim about Transformers. Our finding that WSP does not need Transformer applies to how current LLMs write weights from random initialization without running on data. In that setting, writing requires naming what each weight means, whereas Transformers are built to be trainable with gradient descent. If later method writes weights beyond recall, the best architecture is an open question and should pass our controls (searching written text alone, counting weights actually written, and moving to other benchmarks). Three directions follow, namely writing calculation and comparison into weights, training by gradient descent from written associative-memory-based model, and adding word order so that the model generates text. 12 Preprint. Small-model speed boundary. The associative-memory-based model removes the growth of inference time with the number of facts, but its time grows with the number of concepts. On GPU, its speed advantage over same-sized Transformer therefore holds up to the concept counts measured in Section 6 (between about 15,000 and 32,000 concepts with dense concept table, and about 100,000 with row lists). Hardware for lookup. We measured inference on single GPU model (an RTX 3090) built for dense matrix products, whereas per question our associative-memory-based model computes hashed addresses, reads fixed number of table rows, and accumulates their sparse entries. In recommendation systems, near-memory processing and FPGA engines accelerate such table lookups (Ke et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021), and hash-based sparse CPU execution has outpaced GPUs on large workloads (Chen et al., 2020). Other designs replace inference multiplications with hashing and table lookups (Blalock & Guttag, 2021) or execute associative search directly in content-addressable memory (Ni et al., 2019). Whereas Transformers fit the dense-compute GPUs they co-evolved with (Hooker, 2021), benchmarking written models on lookup-oriented hardware and co-designing the forward pass for it remain open directions. Low-label text and warm-starting. Although we have run no experiment in low-label domains such as medicine or personalization, our text results (Section G) motivate using written networks when labels are scarce. Used to initialize gradient descent on 100 labeled AG News articles, written network reaches up to 84.7% accuracy, whereas training from random initialization on the same labels reaches at most 63.6%. Rubric-guided generational search. Because an LLM can already design its own model structure and revise it across generations, the next step is an automated loop over generations that scores candidate models by rubric combining accuracy per writing cost, model size, and inference speed.

sections.title: 9 Related work
sections.content: Recent work shows that language models can directly read and write network weights without gradient training (Takehi et al., 2026). Earlier work constructs or compiles weights without language model, studying transformer-like computation (Weiss et al., 2021), compiling Transformers for interpretability (Lindner et al., 2023), and hand-constructing factstoring MLPs for Transformers (Dugan et al., 2025). These works fix the architecture and ask what can be written into it, while we leave the structure to the LLM and compare it with the same LLMs Transformers. Other work modifies an already trained model. Where low-rank adaptation updates large language model by gradient training (Hu et al., 2022), model-editing methods locate and edit factual associations in GPT (Meng et al., 2022) and extend those edits to mass-editing memory in Transformer (Meng et al., 2023). Rather than retraining the model, these editing methods compute low-rank weight updates from forward-pass statistics and gradientoptimized target vectors on trained model, whereas our LLMs start from nothing or from random initialization, apart from the pretrained edits of Section 7.1. Prior work also searches over structures or programs and generates weights. With language models, Chen et al. (2023) perform code-level neural architecture search, Nasir et al. (2024) add quality-diversity optimization, and Romera-Paredes et al. (2024) search over programs for mathematical discoveries, while Ha et al. (2016) introduce hypernetworks as networks that generate weights. In the older line of fast weight programmers, slow network trained by gradient descent outputs the weights of second, fast network (Schmidhuber, 1992), and linear Transformers can be written as such fast weight programmers (Schlag et al., 2021). WSP shares only part of the name with fast weight programmers, since in WSP language model writes the weights of separate model itself and the written model receives no gradient training. These search and weight-generation methods train candidate structures with gradients or score many candidates by measured fitness on data, whereas our setup never trains candidate models with gradients. Each run sees only ten labeled example questions 13 Preprint. without benchmark accuracy, and across generations lineage uses one validation accuracy per run only to pass the better of two runs to the next generation. Although existing work reads Transformer layers as associative memories (Zhong et al., 2025; Wang, 2026), Cheng et al. (2026) argue that Transformers lack native lookup primitive and simulate retrieval with computation. Whereas Lample et al. (2019) place productkey memory layers inside Transformer as learned key table read by top-k search, the Engram module of Cheng et al. (2026) adds constant-time lookup beside mixture-of-experts layers, hashing suﬀix N-grams of token ids to addresses in embedding tables pretrained by gradient descent and adding retrieved vectors, gated by the hidden state, to the residual stream. In our associative-memory-based model, the table read at computed address is the whole model rather than Transformer module, keys are concept pairs rather than token N-grams, and an LLM writes entries line by line without gradients.

sections.title: A WSP protocol
sections.content: In this paper, weight-space programming (WSP) denotes the setting in which large language model (LLM) writes the weights of target model by hand, with no gradient training and no fitting on data (Figure 5). target model is forward pass made only of fixed tensor operations. Parameters counts each non-zero entry of dense tensor and, for sparse tensor, each stored value together with its indices; zero entries of dense tensors are stored but not counted. Where table or figure says non-zero values, it counts non-zero entries only, without indices, and same-sized Transformer is one with that number of parameters. neural network such as Transformer is one such target model, and the LLM-designed models are another. We compare models produced by WSP against models trained by gradient descent (GD) using Adam. As in the main text, examples and numbers for single model come from Claude Opus 5.5 and its first-generation models unless another LLM or generation is named. Figure 5: The writer sees only ten ARC examples and, from generation 2, its parent model and its parents validation accuracy; only the host scores benchmark questions; of all scores, only the parents validation accuracy passes to the next generation. On the left, the writer produces its deliverable inside the sandbox. On the right, the host builds and scores each run. Writers and sandbox. The writers are Claude Opus 5.5 at high reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Astra, along with Claude Fable 5.2 where stated. Each writer works with file, search, and shell tools in an isolated sandbox without network access other than to its model. The sandbox contains no project files and no benchmark files except the examples that task allows, and check before each run verifies that no disallowed data file or network connection is present. Task and deliverable. At the start of run, the writer receives task file with the task description, the scoring rule, example items allowed by the task, and the protocol rules. For fixed architectures, the task file also gives the forward pass exactly as evaluated and the name and shape of every weight tensor. In the sandbox, the writer can build the weights from its files, verify parameter names and shapes without running the model on benchmark data, and run the model on CPU. ARC questions are the four-option questions. On ARC, the writer sees five training questions with answers from each of ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge and no other ARC item. For the given Transformer, our associative-memory-based model, and the LLM-designed models, the writer delivers folder containing word list and build script that turns hand-written files into weight tensors, with formulas and loops allowed, plus forward pass when designing the model. For fixed architectures, the given forward pass may not change. For released architecture, the writer delivers an edit script that rewrites the tensors of randomly initialized or pretrained checkpoint; across the 87 released-architecture runs from random initialization of the three writers on ARC, the median run changes 80% of the parameters (range 35% to 100%), and the rest keep their random initial values. The parameter counts reported for these architectures count all of their 19 Preprint. parameters. In free design, where the writer designs the model, static syntax check forbids Python conditionals, while loops, boolean operators, and conversions from tensors to Python scalars or lists, while allowing every tensor operation, including topk, sort, and gather. For the given Transformer, our associative-memory-based model, and the LLMdesigned models, fixed regular-expression tokenizer converts input text into word ids, keeping 128 words for each question and 48 words for each option. Scoring of released architectures uses the releases own tokenizer and the plain prompt Question: A. D. Answer:, reading the larger of the logits of and for each letter at the last token for decoders, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7, and at an appended mask token through the masked-language-model head for encoders. Any question on which all four options receive the same logit counts as one quarter correct for every written model, including released architectures; gradient-descent baselines and prompted pretrained models take the highest logit. Given Transformer. The given Transformer has two pre-norm layers, four attention heads, an MLP width twice the model width, GELU activations, and learned absolute position embeddings. Each option forms one sequence made of the 128 question word ids followed by the 48 option word ids; mean pooling over non-padding tokens and dot product with one score vector gives the option logit. In the main comparison  (Table 3)  , Claude Opus 5.5 writes widths 64, 8, and 24, and GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra write width 64, with additional widths written for the speed comparison. The LLM writes every weight; there are no starting weights. Lineages. lineage runs generations of the same task, where each generation has two runs. Generation 1 has no parent. The protocol allows no gradient training or statistical fitting of any kind on data. During run, the writer never sees accuracy on ARC questions other than its parents single validation accuracy. The writer can run the model on questions it makes up and see its accuracy on them, and writers sometimes use such practice questions to track accuracy; in four runs of Claude Opus 5.5, one of them written Transformer, the writer compared few settings it chose on its own practice questions. On ARC data, the only choice made from 20 Preprint. measured accuracy is selecting the parent of the next generation by validation accuracy; no choice uses the test set. Formulas and code that generate weights from text files that the writer wrote by hand are allowed, whereas computing weights from dataset items is not. Stopping. writing run ends when the writer reports the deliverable finished or reaches fixed budget of output tokens or wall-clock time. Scoring and accounting. Scoring never takes place inside the writers sandbox. After run ends, the deliverable is copied out, built, and evaluated in separate sandbox with no network access on the 3,530 ARC test questions, which the writer never saw. On ARC, the memory limit given to the writer is 2 GB for models other than released architectures, and scoring enforces 6 GB and 20 minutes (16 GB for released architectures). C.3 Final-generation models In generation 5, Claude Opus 5.5 writes plain sentences with single science fact per line. sections.title: D Controls on the written models
sections.content: Test-set overlap. The text written by each LLM overlaps the ARC test set about as often as comparable questions that the LLM did not see, and deleting the overlapping lines barely changes test accuracy  (Table 13)  . Across all three lineages, overlap on ARC test matches the low rate on the ARC training questions that the LLM never saw during the run and on external science benchmarks. In this test, an item is the question stem followed by its correct option in lowercase word tokens, and written artifact is every line of every file in the model folder. An item is flagged if any of four rules fires. Under the first rule, any word 11-gram of an ARC-Easy item, 12-gram of an ARC-Challenge item, or 13-gram of another item occurs in one line (Brown et al., 2020). Under the second rule, at least 70% of the items 8-grams occur in the artifact (Chowdhery et al., 2022). Under the third rule, the longest token span shared with one line covers at least half of the item (Singh et al., 2024); the 0.5 threshold is ours. The fourth rule is ours, with content words defined as tokens other than stopwords and digits. For items with at least five content words, it fires when one line holds at least 80% of the items content words and every content word of its correct option. The deletion test follows Gunasekar et al. (2023). When Claude Opus 5.5 guesses masked option from an item stem, exact match is 15.3% on ARC test. The same probe reaches 16.3% on ARC training items, so Claude Opus 5.5 recalls masked ARC test options no more often than ARC training options.
